paragraphs: The first of these errands was at Madame Hohlakov’s house, and he hurried there to get it over with and not be too late for Mitya. Madame Hohlakov had been slightly unwell for the last three weeks. Her foot had swollen up for some reason, and though she was not in bed, she spent all day half-reclining on the couch in her boudoir, in a fascinating but decorous _déshabillé_. Alyosha had once noticed with innocent amusement that, in spite of her illness, Madame Hohlakov had started dressing up rather a lot. Top-knots, ribbons and loose wrappers had made their appearance. He had an inkling of the reason, though he dismissed such thoughts from his mind as frivolous. For the last two months the young official, Perhotin, had been a regular visitor at the house.

Alyosha had not called for four days and was in a hurry to go straight to Lise, since it was with her that he had to speak. Lise had sent a maid to him the day before, specially asking him to come to her “about something very important,” a request that, for certain reasons, interested Alyosha. But while the maid went to announce him to Lise, Madame Hohlakov heard of his arrival from someone and immediately sent to ask him to come to her “just for one minute.” Alyosha thought it better to give in to the mamma’s request, or else she would keep sending down to Lise’s room every minute he was there. Madame Hohlakov was lying on a couch. She was especially smartly dressed and was clearly in a state of extreme nervous excitement. She greeted Alyosha with cries of delight.

“It’s ages, ages, absolutely ages since I’ve seen you! It’s a whole week—just think of it! Ah, but you were here only four days ago, on Wednesday. You’ve come to see Lise. I’m sure you meant to slip into her room on tiptoe, without my hearing you. My dear, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, if you only knew how worried I am about her! But more of that later, though it’s the most important thing, more of that later. Dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, I trust you completely with my Lise. Since the death of Father Zossima—God rest his soul!” (she crossed herself)—“I look on you as a monk, though you look charming in your new suit. Where did you find such a tailor in these parts? No, no, that’s not the main thing—more of that later. Forgive me for sometimes calling you Alyosha; an old woman like me can take liberties,” she smiled coquettishly; “but that can wait too. The important thing is that I shouldn’t forget what is important. Please remind me yourself. As soon as my tongue runs away with me, just say ‘the important thing?’ Ach! How do I know now what matters most? Ever since Lise took back her promise—her childish promise, Alexey Fyodorovitch—to marry you, you’ve realized, of course, that it was only the playful fancy of a sick child who had been confined to her chair so long—thank God, she can walk now!... that new doctor Katya sent for from Moscow for your unhappy brother, who tomorrow will—But why speak of tomorrow? I’m ready to die at the very thought of tomorrow. Ready to die of curiosity.... That doctor was with us yesterday and saw Lise.... I paid him fifty roubles for the visit. But that’s not the point, that’s not the point again. You see, I’m mixing everything up. I’m in such a hurry. Why am I in a hurry? I don’t understand. It’s awful how I seem to be losing the ability to understand anything. Everything seems mixed up in a sort of tangle. I’m afraid you’re so bored you’ll jump up and run away, and that will be all I see of you. Goodness! Why are we sitting here with no coffee? Yulia, Glafira, coffee!”
Alyosha quickly thanked her and said he had only just had coffee.
“Where?”
“At Agrafena Alexandrovna’s.”

“At ... at that woman’s? Ah, she’s the one who’s ruined everyone. I know nothing about it, though. They say she’s become a saint, though it’s rather late in the day. She should have done it before. What use is it now? Hush, hush, Alexey Fyodorovitch, because I have so much to say to you that I’m afraid I’ll tell you nothing. This awful trial ... I’ll certainly go, I’m making arrangements. I’ll be carried there in my chair; besides, I can sit up. I’ll have people with me. And, you know, I’m a witness. How will I speak, how will I speak? I don’t know what I’ll say. One has to take an oath, doesn’t one?”
“Yes, but I don’t think you’ll be able to go.”

“I can sit up. Ah, you’ve thrown me off! Ah! This trial, this savage act, and then they’re all going to Siberia, some are getting married, and all so quickly, so quickly, everything’s changing, and at last—nothing. Everyone grows old with death to look forward to. Well, so be it! I’m weary. This Katya, _cette charmante personne_, has dashed all my hopes. Now she’s going to follow one of your brothers to Siberia, and your other brother is going to follow her and live in the nearest town, and they’ll all torment one another. It drives me out of my mind. Worst of all—the publicity. The story has been told a million times over in all the papers in Moscow and Petersburg. Ah! Yes, would you believe it, there’s an item saying I was ‘a dear friend’ of your brother’s ——, I can’t repeat the horrid word. Just imagine, just imagine!”
“Impossible! Where was the item? What did it say?”

“I’ll show you in a minute. I got the paper and read it yesterday. Here, in the Petersburg paper _Gossip_. The paper started coming out this year. I’m awfully fond of gossip, so I subscribe, and now it pays me back—this is what gossip comes to! Here it is, this passage. Read it.”
And she handed Alyosha a sheet of newspaper that had been under her pillow.

It was not exactly that she was upset; she seemed overwhelmed, and perhaps everything really was tangled in her head. The item was very typical and must have been a great shock to her. But, fortunately perhaps, she could not keep her mind fixed on any one subject at that moment, and so might race off in a minute to something else and forget the newspaper entirely.

Alyosha was well aware that the story of the terrible case had spread all over Russia. And, good heavens, what wild rumors about his brother, about the Karamazovs and about himself he had read in those two months, among other equally credible items! One paper had even stated that he had gone into a monastery and become a monk, in horror at his brother’s crime. Another contradicted this and stated that he and his elder, Father Zossima, had broken into the monastery chest and “made tracks from the monastery.” The present item in _Gossip_ was headed “The Karamazov Case at Skotoprigonyevsk.” (That, alas, was the name of our little town. I had kept it hidden until now.) It was brief, and Madame Hohlakov was not mentioned in it directly. No names appeared, in fact. It said only that the criminal, whose approaching trial was causing such a sensation—a retired army captain, an idle swaggerer and reactionary bully—was constantly involved in amorous intrigues and was especially popular with certain ladies “who were pining in solitude.” One such lady, a pining widow who tried to seem young though she had a grown-up daughter, was so taken with him that only two hours before the crime she offered him three thousand roubles, on condition that he elope with her to the gold mines. But the criminal, counting on escaping punishment, had preferred to murder his father to get the three thousand rather than go off to Siberia with the middle-aged charms of his pining lady. This playful item ended, of course, with an outburst of generous indignation at the wickedness of parricide and at the recently abolished institution of serfdom. Reading it with curiosity, Alyosha folded up the paper and handed it back to Madame Hohlakov.

“Well, that must be me,” she hurried on again. “Of course I’m the one meant. Barely an hour before, I suggested gold mines to him, and here they talk of ‘middle-aged charms’ as though that were my motive! He writes that out of spite! God Almighty forgive him for the middle-aged charms, as I forgive him! You know it’s— Do you know who it is? It’s your friend Rakitin.”
“Perhaps,” said Alyosha, “though I’ve heard nothing about it.”
“It’s he, it’s he! No ‘perhaps’ about it. You know I turned him out of the house.... You know that whole story, don’t you?”
“I know you asked him not to visit you anymore, but I haven’t heard why ... from you, at least.”
“Ah, so you’ve heard it from him! He runs me down, I suppose, runs me down dreadfully?”
“Yes, he does; but then he runs down everyone. But why you’ve given him up I haven’t heard from him either. I meet him very seldom now, in fact. We’re not friends.”

“Well, then, I’ll tell you all about it. There’s no help for it, I’ll confess, because there is one point on which I was perhaps to blame. Only a little, little point, so little that perhaps it doesn’t count. You see, my dear boy”—Madame Hohlakov suddenly looked arch, and a charming though enigmatic smile played about her lips—“you see, I suspect ... You must forgive me, Alyosha. I’m like a mother to you.... No, no; quite the contrary. I speak to you now as though you were my father—mother’s quite out of place. Well, it’s as though I were confessing to Father Zossima, that’s just it. I called you a monk just now. Well, that poor young man, your friend Rakitin (Mercy on us! I can’t be angry with him. I feel cross, but not very), that frivolous young man, would you believe it, seems to have taken it into his head to fall in love with me. I only noticed it later. At first—a month ago—he only began to come to see me more often, almost every day, though of course we were acquainted before. I knew nothing about it ... and suddenly it dawned on me, and I began to notice things with surprise. You know, two months ago, that modest, charming, excellent young man, Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, who’s in the service here, began to be a regular visitor at the house. You met him here ever so many times yourself. And he’s an excellent, earnest young man, isn’t he? He comes once every three days, not every day (though I’d be glad to see him every day), and always so well dressed. Altogether, I love young people, Alyosha, talented, modest ones, like you, and he has almost the mind of a statesman, he talks so charmingly, and I shall certainly, certainly try to get him promoted. He’s a future diplomat. On that awful day he almost saved me from death by coming in the night. And your friend Rakitin comes in such boots, and always stretches them out on the carpet.... He began hinting at his feelings, in fact, and one day, as he was leaving, he squeezed my hand terribly hard. My foot began to swell right after he pressed my hand like that. He had met Pyotr Ilyitch here before, and would you believe it, he’s always gibing at him, growling at him, for some reason. I simply watched how they went on together and laughed inwardly. So I was sitting here alone—no, I was laid up then. Well, I was lying here alone and suddenly Rakitin comes in, and just imagine! He brought me some verses of his own composition—a short poem, on my bad foot: that is, he described my foot in a poem. Wait a minute—how did it go?
A captivating little foot.

It began somehow like that. I can never remember poetry. I’ve got it here. I’ll show it to you later. But it’s a charming thing—charming; and, you know, it’s not only about the foot, it had a good moral too, a charming idea, only I’ve forgotten it; in fact, it was just the thing for an album. So, of course, I thanked him, and he was clearly flattered. I’d hardly had time to thank him when Pyotr Ilyitch came in, and Rakitin suddenly looked black as night. I could see that Pyotr Ilyitch was in the way, because Rakitin certainly wanted to say something after giving me the verses. I had a feeling he did; but then Pyotr Ilyitch came in. I showed Pyotr Ilyitch the verses and didn’t say who the author was. But I’m convinced he guessed, though he won’t admit it to this day and says he had no idea. But he says that on purpose. Pyotr Ilyitch began to laugh at once and fell to criticizing them. ‘Wretched doggerel,’ he said they were, ‘some divinity student must have written them,’ and with such vehemence, such vehemence! Then, instead of laughing, your friend flew into a rage. ‘Good gracious!’ I thought, ‘they’re going to fly at each other.’ ‘I wrote them,’ he said. ‘I wrote them as a joke,’ he said, ‘because I think it degrading to write verses.... But they’re good poetry. They want to put up a monument to your Pushkin for writing about women’s feet, while I wrote with a moral purpose, and you,’ he said, ‘are an advocate of serfdom. You’ve no humane ideas,’ he said. ‘You have no modern enlightened feelings, you’re untouched by progress, you’re a mere official,’ he said, ‘and you take bribes.’ Then I began screaming and begging them to stop. And, you know, Pyotr Ilyitch is anything but a coward. He at once took the most gentlemanly tone, looked at him sarcastically, listened, and apologized. ‘I had no idea,’ he said. ‘I wouldn’t have said it if I’d known. I’d have praised them. Poets are all so irritable,’ he said. In short, he laughed at him under cover of the most gentlemanly tone. He explained to me afterwards that it was all sarcasm. I thought he was in earnest. Only as I lay there, just as I am now before you, I thought, ‘Would it, or would it not, be the proper thing for me to turn Rakitin out for shouting so rudely at a visitor in my house?’ And, would you believe it, I lay here, shut my eyes, and wondered whether it would be the proper thing or not. I kept worrying and worrying, and my heart began to pound, and I couldn’t make up my mind whether to make an outcry or not. One voice seemed to be telling me, ‘Speak,’ and the other, ‘No, don’t speak.’ And no sooner had the second voice said that than I cried out, and fainted. Of course, there was a fuss. I got up suddenly and said to Rakitin, ‘It’s painful for me to say it, but I don’t wish to see you in my house again.’ So I turned him out. Ah! Alexey Fyodorovitch, I know myself I did wrong. I was putting it on. I wasn’t angry with him at all, really; but I suddenly imagined—that was what did it—that it would make such a fine scene.... And yet, believe me, it was quite natural, because I really shed tears and cried for several days afterwards, and then suddenly, one afternoon, I forgot all about it. So it’s two weeks since he’s been here, and I kept wondering whether he’d come again. I wondered even yesterday, and then suddenly last night came this _Gossip_. I read it and gasped. Who could have written it? He must have written it. He went home, sat down, wrote it on the spot, sent it, and they printed it. It was two weeks ago, you see. But, Alyosha, it’s awful how I keep talking and don’t say what I want to say. Ah! The words come of themselves!”
